tags.label: Application
tags.test: The snapshot is used to build general application software end to end.

tags.label: Systems
tags.test: The snapshot is used to build operating-system components, drivers, runtimes, or other close-to-hardware software.

tags.label: Web front end
tags.test: The snapshot is used to build code that runs in a web browser and drives a user interface.

tags.label: Web back end
tags.test: The snapshot is used to build server-side services that answer network requests.

tags.label: Desktop
tags.test: The snapshot is used to build windowed applications for a desktop operating system.

tags.label: Mobile
tags.test: The snapshot is used to build applications for a mobile operating system.

tags.label: Embedded
tags.test: The snapshot is used to build software for microcontrollers, bare hardware, or real-time targets.

tags.label: Data and statistics
tags.test: The snapshot is used to analyse, model, or visualise data as its main task.

tags.label: Scripting
tags.test: The snapshot is used to automate tasks and glue other programs together.

tags.label: Command shell
tags.test: The snapshot is used as an interactive command language at a terminal.

tags.label: Query
tags.test: The snapshot is used to declare, query, or manipulate stored data.

tags.label: Verification
tags.test: The snapshot is used to prove properties of programs, or to build software under a certification regime.

tags.label: Education
tags.test: The snapshot is used mainly to teach programming.

tags.label: Blockchain
tags.test: The snapshot is used to write programs that execute on a blockchain.

tags.label: Object-oriented
tags.test: The snapshot provides classes or objects with inheritance or dynamic dispatch as a primary structuring device.

tags.label: Functional
tags.test: The snapshot treats functions as first-class values and makes recursion and immutability central.

tags.label: Imperative
tags.test: The snapshot expresses computation as statements that assign and mutate state.

tags.label: Procedural
tags.test: The snapshot structures programs as named subprograms called in sequence.

tags.label: Declarative
tags.test: The snapshot states what a result is rather than the steps that produce it.

tags.label: Logic
tags.test: The snapshot derives answers by resolution over facts and rules.

tags.label: Concurrent
tags.test: The snapshot provides language-level constructs for concurrent execution.

tags.label: Array
tags.test: The snapshot operates on whole arrays as the primary unit of expression.

tags.label: JVM
tags.test: The snapshot's programs run on the Java Virtual Machine.

tags.label: CLR
tags.test: The snapshot's programs run on the .NET common language runtime.

tags.label: BEAM
tags.test: The snapshot's programs run on the BEAM virtual machine.

tags.label: Native
tags.test: The snapshot compiles to native machine code for the host platform.

tags.label: Browser
tags.test: The snapshot's programs run inside a web browser engine.

tags.label: Node.js
tags.test: The snapshot's programs run on a server-side JavaScript runtime such as Node.js, Deno, or Bun.

tags.label: WebAssembly
tags.test: The snapshot compiles to WebAssembly as a first-class target.

tags.label: Embedded target
tags.test: The snapshot runs on bare hardware or a real-time operating system.

tags.label: Mobile target
tags.test: The snapshot runs on iOS or Android as a supported deployment target.

tags.label: EVM
tags.test: The snapshot's programs execute on the Ethereum Virtual Machine.

tags.label: Current
tags.test: The snapshot is the family's newest stable release at the date of publication.

tags.label: Supported
tags.test: The snapshot is an older release still maintained or still shipping.

tags.label: Superseded
tags.test: A newer release of the same family has replaced the snapshot.

tags.label: Frozen
tags.test: The snapshot is a standard or release that no longer changes.

tags.label: Retired
tags.test: The snapshot is withdrawn or officially discontinued.

tags.label: Preview
tags.test: The snapshot is a pre-1.0 or alpha line that is not yet declared stable.

tags.label: Managed (GC)
tags.test: A garbage collector reclaims memory and no explicit deallocation is required.

tags.label: Runtime-managed
tags.test: The runtime allocates and reclaims storage implicitly, with neither a tracing collector nor explicit deallocation in the language.

tags.label: Manual
tags.test: The program decides when memory is released, through an explicit call or a scope rule.

tags.label: Ownership
tags.test: A compile-time ownership and borrow discipline decides when memory is reclaimed.

tags.label: Reference counted
tags.test: Reference counts decide when an object's memory is reclaimed.

tags.label: Static, strong
tags.test: Types are checked before execution, without T1 or T2 in the snapshot's verdicts.

tags.label: Static, weak
tags.test: Types are checked before execution, but T2 (weak static) is present in the snapshot's verdicts.

tags.label: Dynamic
tags.test: Types are checked at run time; T1 (dynamic, no static check) is present in the snapshot's verdicts.
